title: Components, images, and equal Lie algebras
statement:
Fix an algebraically closed field $L$ of characteristic zero. In this statement an algebraic group is a group scheme of finite type over $L$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], as in the standing convention of the current blueprint's sk-i-cartier. Connected components refer to the underlying topological space [def-weil-connected-scheme]; the identity component has its open-and-closed subscheme structure. Write $\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_{G/L,1}$ for the tangent space at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. For a closed subgroup scheme $K\hookrightarrow G$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], equality $\operatorname{Lie}(K)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ means that the differential of this inclusion identifies the two tangent spaces, using the canonical Lie algebra and differential of [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation].

An algebraic group $G$ has finitely many connected components. Its
identity component $G^\circ$ is an open, closed, irreducible normal
subgroup, and the other components are its cosets. The image of a
homomorphism of algebraic groups is a closed subgroup. If $G$ is connected
and $K\subseteq G$ is a closed subgroup scheme with $\Lie(K)=\Lie(G)$,
then $K=G$.

*Complement.* For closed subgroups of $\GL(V)$ the image on $L$-points of a
regular homomorphism $G\to K$ is the set of $L$-points of a closed
subgroup of $K$, taken with its reduced structure; and if $G$ is connected
and a closed subgroup $J\subseteq G$ has $\dim J=\dim G$, then $J=G$.

In the image assertion, for a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ the underlying image $f(|G|)$ is closed in $|H|$ and its reduced induced closed subscheme is a subgroup scheme; its $L$-points are exactly $f(G(L))$ [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme, def-weil-field-valued-points]. Matrix groups and their regular homomorphisms in the complement use [sk-d-geometry].

proof.text: Finite type over the Noetherian scheme $\operatorname{Spec}L$ makes $G$ Noetherian. Hence there are finitely many irreducible components. Each irreducible component is connected and is contained in one connected component: the union of two intersecting connected subsets is connected. Conversely every point lies on an irreducible component. Thus every connected component is a union of members of this finite family, and there are finitely many connected components.

Cartier smoothness applies to $G$ over the characteristic-zero field $L$. Its local rings are therefore regular and hence domains. If distinct irreducible components met at $x$, choose an affine neighbourhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $x$. Their intersections with $U$ are distinct irreducible components of $U$, hence correspond to distinct minimal primes $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak m_x$. The prime correspondence for $A_{\mathfrak m_x}\cong\mathcal O_{G,x}$ sends them to distinct minimal primes of this domain, impossible since its sole minimal prime is $(0)$. The finite irreducible components are consequently disjoint. Each is closed and its complement is a finite union of closed components, so each is open. A connected subset cannot cross such a partition; hence these are exactly the connected components. In particular the identity component $C$ is irreducible.

Give $C$ its open subscheme structure. The general identity-component theorem supplies geometric irreducibility of $C$ and its subgroup scheme structure; it applies to a group scheme locally of finite type over the algebraically closed field $L$. For each component $D$, a nonempty affine open of $D$ has a closed point, and the affine Nullstellensatz makes that point $L$-rational. Choose it as $g$. Translation is an isomorphism sending $1$ to $g$, so it sends the whole connected component $C$ onto $D$. Thus the components are precisely the cosets $gC$. To check normality as a subgroup scheme, decompose $G\times_L C$ into the open pieces $gC\times_L C$. Each is isomorphic to $C\times_L C$, which is irreducible by geometric irreducibility. The conjugation map $(a,c)\mapsto aca^{-1}$ sends each such piece to a connected subset containing $1$ (take $c=1$), hence into $C$. It therefore factors through the open subscheme $C$. The factorization proves scheme-theoretic normality, including points with values in arbitrary $L$-algebras.

source.place: First paragraph, subgroup, cosets and normality

proof.text: Let $f:G\to H$ be a homomorphism, and let $J$ be the reduced induced closed subscheme on $\overline{f(|G|)}\subseteq H$. Regard a group scheme as an absolute groupoid with object scheme $\operatorname{Spec}L$: both structure maps are the map to $\operatorname{Spec}L$, and composition is multiplication. The groupoid image-closure theorem over the perfect field $L$ gives $J$ the restricted group operations, with $J\hookrightarrow H$ a homomorphism. This is precisely a closed subgroup scheme. Cartier makes $G$ reduced; the reduced-source factorization theorem therefore factors $f$ through $J$. Denote the factor by $q:G\to J$. Since the closed immersion $J\hookrightarrow H$ is a monomorphism, compatibility of $q$ with the group laws follows from compatibility of $f$. The image $S=q(|G|)$ is dense in $J$ by its construction.

source.place: Second paragraph, closure is a subgroup

proof.text: The schemes $G,H,J$ are of finite type over $L$: locally $J$ is defined by a quotient of a finite-type coordinate algebra of $H$, and it is quasi-compact as a closed subset of the Noetherian scheme $H$. They are Noetherian. The map $q$ is locally of finite type: for affine charts $\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq G$ mapping to $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq J$, any finite set of $L$-algebra generators for $B$ also generates it as an $A$-algebra. Its inverse images of affine opens are open in Noetherian $G$, hence quasi-compact. Since $J$ is locally Noetherian, $q$ is locally of finite presentation. Apply Chevalley to $q$: $J$ is quasi-compact and separated, hence quasi-separated, so $S$ is constructible. Choose a nonempty affine open $A_0\subseteq J$. The set $S\cap A_0$ is dense and constructible in $A_0$. Part (2) of the affine constructible-open lemma gives a nonempty open $U\subseteq A_0$ contained in $S\cap A_0$. Thus $U$ is open in $J$ and $U\subseteq S$.

source.place: Second paragraph, Chevalley and an open piece

proof.text: Put $P=q(G(L))\subseteq J(L)$, a subgroup. For every $u\in U(L)$ the fibre $G_u$ is nonempty since $U\subseteq S$. It is of finite type over $L$, by base change of the finite-type morphism $q$. A nonempty affine open in this fibre has a closed point; the affine Nullstellensatz identifies its residue field with $L$. Hence $u$ lifts to $G(L)$, and $U(L)\subseteq P$. The same argument applied to a nonempty affine open in $U$ shows $U(L)\ne\varnothing$; choose $u_0$ in it. Set $W=u_0^{-1}U$, an open neighbourhood of $1$ in $J$. Translation is an isomorphism, and $W(L)=u_0^{-1}U(L)\subseteq P$.

source.place: Second paragraph, passage from scheme image to L-points

proof.text: In the subspace topology on $J(L)$ one has $P=\bigcup_{p\in P}pW(L)$, so $P$ is open. Every coset $aP$ is open by translation; the complement of $P$, the union of its other cosets, is therefore open too. Thus $P$ is closed in $J(L)$. Cartier makes $G$ smooth, so rational-point density gives $\overline{G(L)}=|G|$. Continuity of $q$ implies $q(|G|)\subseteq\overline{q(G(L))}$, so $P$ is dense in $J$ and in $J(L)$. Consequently $P=J(L)$. This uses translations on rational points only; it does not assume that the Zariski topology on the scheme product is the product of the two underlying topological spaces.

source.place: Second paragraph, open subgroup and its cosets

proof.text: It remains to check the underlying scheme image. The complement $J\setminus S$ is constructible, being the complement of a constructible subset of a Noetherian space. If nonempty, one of its locally closed pieces is nonempty. Choose a nonempty affine open in that locally closed subscheme, then a closed point in that affine open. Its residue field is $L$ by the affine Nullstellensatz, so its image gives an $L$-point of $J\setminus S$. This contradicts $P=J(L)$ and $P\subseteq S$. Thus $S=|J|$. The original homomorphism has closed underlying image, equipped with the reduced subgroup structure $J$, and its image on $L$-points is exactly $J(L)$. This proves both the image assertion and the matrix-group complement, with no affineness assumption on the groups in the first assertion.

source.place: Second paragraph, closedness as a scheme subset

proof.text:
Suppose now that $G$ is connected and $K\hookrightarrow G$ is the given closed subgroup scheme with bijective differential at $1$. The schemes $G$ and $K$ are smooth by Cartier (a closed subgroup of a finite-type group is finite type). For each of the two groups, the Lie algebra of the smooth Lie-local-dimension theorem is $L$-linearly equivalent, after the canonical identity residue-field identification, to its dual-number tangent space at the identity ($T_{K/L,1}$, resp. $T_{G/L,1}$) used in the statement; so the vector-space dimensions agree. Apply the smooth Lie-local-dimension theorem and the identity-local-dimension theorem to each group. They give
$\dim K=\dim\mathcal O_{K,1}=\dim_L\operatorname{Lie}(K)=\dim_L\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\dim\mathcal O_{G,1}=\dim G$.
The middle equality is induced by the differential of the inclusion, not by an unspecified identification of abstract Lie algebras. By the component argument above, connected $G$ is irreducible. Its dimension is finite by finite type over $L$.

source.place: Third paragraph, equality of dimensions from equal Lie algebras

proof.text: If the closed support of $K$ were proper in irreducible $G$, it would be nowhere dense: a nonempty open in an irreducible space is dense. The finite-dimensional Noetherian dimension-drop lemma would give $\dim K<\dim G$, contradicting the preceding equality. Thus $K$ and $G$ have the same underlying support. Both are reduced by Cartier, and uniqueness of the reduced induced closed subscheme on that support identifies $K$ with $G$ as closed subschemes. For the dimension version of the complement, start instead with the assumed equality $\dim J=\dim G$; the same support argument and Cartier reducedness apply directly. This also covers zero-dimensional connected groups.

source.place: Third paragraph, dimension drop and reduced scheme equality

blueprint_update.statement:
An algebraic group $G$ has finitely many connected components. Its
identity component $G^\circ$ is an open, closed, irreducible normal
subgroup, and the other components are its cosets. The image of a
homomorphism of algebraic groups is closed. If $G$ is connected and
$J\subseteq G$ is a closed subgroup scheme with $\dim J=\dim G$, then
$J=G$.

For closed subgroups $G\subseteq\GL(V)$ and $G'\subseteq\GL(W)$, the
image $f(G(L))$ of a regular homomorphism $f\colon G\to G'$ is the set of
$L$-points of a closed subgroup of $G'$, taken with its reduced
structure. If $G\subseteq\GL(V)$ is a connected closed subgroup and
$K\subseteq G$ is a closed subgroup with $\Lie(K)=\Lie(G)$, then $K=G$.

proof.text:
Since $G$ is Noetherian, it has finitely many irreducible components. By
[sk-i-cartier], the scheme $G$ is smooth, and since a regular local ring is
a domain, distinct irreducible components of $G$ do not meet. Hence the
irreducible components are open and closed, and they are exactly the
connected components. Multiplication and inversion map the component
containing $1$ to itself, so it is a subgroup, and conjugation preserves
it. Translations identify the other components with its cosets.

Let $f\colon G\to G'$ be a homomorphism. By continuity of multiplication
and inversion, the closure $J$ of its image is a subgroup. Chevalley's
theorem ([Stacks 054K](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054K)) says
that $f(G)$ is constructible, and a dense constructible subset contains a
nonempty open subset of its closure. Thus the subgroup $f(G)(L)$ contains
the $L$-points of a nonempty open $U\subseteq J$. Translating $U$ by the
inverse of one of its points in the image, we obtain an open neighbourhood
of $1$ contained in the image, and translating further by points of the
image, we see that the image is open in $J$. Its complement is a union of
cosets of this open subgroup, hence open as well. Therefore the image is
closed, and since it is dense in $J$, it is equal to $J$. For closed
subgroups $G\subseteq\GL(V)$ and $G'\subseteq\GL(W)$, take $J$ with its
reduced structure: since $J\times J$ is reduced and multiplication and
inversion preserve $J(L)$, they restrict to $J$, so $J$ is a closed
subgroup of $G'$, and $f(G(L))=J(L)$.

Next, let $J\subseteq G$ be as in the dimension criterion, with $G$
connected. By the first part, $G$ is irreducible. Since a proper closed
subset of the irreducible variety $G$ has smaller dimension, $J$ and $G$
have the same underlying closed subset. Both are reduced by
[sk-i-cartier], and hence they are equal as schemes.

Finally, let $K\subseteq G\subseteq\GL(V)$ be as in the last assertion.
By Cartier's theorem [sk-i-cartier],
$\dim K=\dim\Lie(K)=\dim\Lie(G)=\dim G$, so $K=G$ by the dimension
criterion.
